Brazilian officials had previously inquired with Apple regarding gambling apps accessible to minors. Nearly three months later, Apple has been asked to provide further information within five business days on the protective measures in its App Store. Details are as follows.

Apple Faces Pressure Over Regulatory and Age Verification Issues

In April last year, Brazilian officials issued notices to both Apple and Google, accusing the two companies' app stores of lacking age restrictions on gambling apps.

At the time, the National Secretariat for Digital Rights (Sedigi) and the National Consumer Secretariat (Senacon) wrote to both companies separately, expressing concern about the "large number of apps" that provided or facilitated minors' access to gambling platforms.

Brazil recently passed a new law known as "ECA Digital," which requires app stores to restrict minors' access to gambling content. Apple subsequently rolled out age verification measures locally for apps rated 18+.

However, officials stated that preliminary investigations found that multiple gambling apps appeared to lack proper age restrictions or federal authorisation, casting doubt on the actual effectiveness of the relevant protective measures.

Although Apple's response lacked transparency, the relevant departments noted that Apple had answered most of the initial questions, but still requested further information from the company.

The following is the content released by the Brazilian Ministry of Justice and Public Security (via Canaltech):

The clarification items requested by the authorities include: how regulatory authorisation is verified for apps listed in Brazil; the technical criteria used to distinguish simulation apps from those involving real-money gambling, including situations where functionality is hidden or altered after approval; and mechanisms to prevent minors from accessing inappropriate content. Information was also requested regarding active monitoring procedures, risk prioritisation criteria, average takedown time after discovery, and the publication of a timeline for implementing remediation measures—including a so-called

The Secretariat noted that Google's response was relatively weak and has requested more detailed explanations, including how the identity of authorised operators is verified, how apps whose licences have been suspended or expired are monitored, how enforcement effectiveness is measured, and how minors are prevented from searching for or downloading gambling apps.

Finally, the Secretariat requested that the responses from Apple and Google be made public, but allowed confidential information to be submitted separately in a restricted format.
